detail: New Jersey v. T.L.O., 469 U.S. 325 (1985). Argued March 28, 1984; reargued October 2, 1984; decided January 15, 1985. Docket No. 83-712.

claim: The subject was a 14-year-old freshman referred to by initials
detail: The student was a 14-year-old high-school freshman. Because she was a minor (juvenile), the court records identify her only by her initials, T.L.O. R2 subject: symbol only, no name beyond the public initials, no likeness.
sources: Cornell LII, 469 U.S. 325 (opinion of the Court, Part I)

claim: A teacher found two girls smoking in a school restroom
detail: A teacher at a New Jersey public high school entered a girls' lavatory (restroom) and discovered two students smoking, in violation of a school rule. One of the two was T.L.O. The teacher took both students to the front/principal's office.

claim: T.L.O. denied smoking; denied she smoked at all
detail: An assistant vice principal questioned T.L.O. She denied she had been smoking in the restroom, and further claimed that she did not smoke at all.

claim: The assistant vice principal searched her purse and found cigarettes, then rolling papers
detail: The assistant vice principal (identified in the record as Theodore Choplick) demanded to see T.L.O.'s purse. Opening it, he found a pack of cigarettes on top; as he removed them he noticed a package of cigarette rolling papers, which in his experience were associated with the use of marijuana. The rolling papers in plain view are the doctrinal hinge that justified continuing the search.

claim: A further search of the purse produced evidence of marijuana dealing
detail: Continuing to search the purse, the official found a small amount of marijuana, a pipe, empty plastic bags, a substantial quantity of money in one-dollar bills, an index card listing students who owed T.L.O. money, and two letters implicating her in marijuana dealing. AD-SAFE FRAMING: reference the escalating findings factually as the reason the search expanded; do not sensationalize or glamorize drugs.

claim: She was adjudicated delinquent after the juvenile court denied suppression
detail: The State brought delinquency charges in juvenile court. T.L.O. moved to suppress the evidence found in her purse, arguing the search violated the Fourth Amendment. The juvenile court denied the motion to suppress, adjudged her a delinquent, and (on January 8, 1982) sentenced her to one year's probation. The New Jersey Supreme Court later reversed and ordered the evidence suppressed; the U.S. Supreme Court then reversed the New Jersey Supreme Court.
sources: Cornell LII, 469 U.S. 325 (opinion, Part I; procedural history)

claim: Question presented: does the Fourth Amendment apply to searches by public-school officials, and by what standard
detail: The case asked whether the Fourth Amendment's prohibition on unreasonable searches and seizures applies to searches conducted by PUBLIC-SCHOOL officials, and, if so, what standard governs such searches.

claim: HOLDING part 1: the Fourth Amendment DOES apply to public-school officials
detail: The Court held that the Fourth Amendment's prohibition on unreasonable searches and seizures applies to searches conducted by public-school officials, who act as representatives of the State, not merely as surrogates for parents. Students do NOT shed their Fourth Amendment protection at the schoolhouse door. BLOCKER: do not say the 4A does not apply or that students have no rights.

claim: HOLDING part 2: no warrant and no probable cause required; standard is reasonableness / reasonable suspicion
detail: The Court held that school officials need NOT obtain a warrant before searching a student, and need NOT be held to the probable-cause standard. The legality of a search of a student depends instead on the REASONABLENESS, under all the circumstances, of the search. Commentators and the Court's framework describe the operative threshold as reasonable suspicion (reasonable grounds), a standard lower than probable cause. BLOCKER: the standard is LOWERED, not eliminated.

VERBATIM: "Determining the reasonableness of any search involves a twofold inquiry: first, one must consider whether the ... action was justified at its inception; second, one must determine whether the search as actually conducted was reasonably related in scope to the circumstances which justified the interference in the first place." PRONG 1 (inception): a search is justified at its inception "when there are reasonable grounds for suspecting that the search will turn up evidence that the student has violated or is violating either the law or the rules of the school." PRONG 2 (scope): a search is permissible in scope "when the measures adopted are reasonably related to the objectives of the search and not excessively intrusive in light of the age and sex of the student and the nature of the infraction."
sources: Cornell LII, 469 U.S. 325 (opinion, Part II) — quoted verbatim

claim: Application: the search of T.L.O.'s purse was reasonable
detail: Applying the two-prong test, the Court held the search was reasonable. The teacher's report of smoking gave reasonable grounds to suspect the purse contained cigarettes, justifying the initial opening (prong 1). Discovery of the rolling papers in plain view then gave reasonable suspicion of marijuana, justifying the more thorough search that turned up the dealing evidence, and the search was not excessively intrusive (prong 2).
The judgment (reversing the New Jersey Supreme Court and upholding the search as reasonable) was reached 6-3.

claim: Exact lineup: White for the Court; concurrences; three concurring in part / dissenting in part
detail: WHITE, J., delivered the opinion of the Court, in which BURGER, C.J., and REHNQUIST, O'CONNOR, and POWELL, JJ., joined (5). POWELL, J., filed a concurring opinion, in which O'CONNOR, J., joined. BLACKMUN, J., filed an opinion concurring in the judgment (the 6th vote for the judgment). BRENNAN, J., filed an opinion concurring in part and dissenting in part, in which MARSHALL, J., joined. STEVENS, J., filed an opinion concurring in part and dissenting in part, in which MARSHALL, J., joined, and in which BRENNAN, J., joined as to Part I. The three who dissented in part from the reasonableness holding are Brennan, Marshall, and Stevens; their principal objection was to lowering the standard below probable cause and/or to the Court's application finding this search reasonable.

claim: The Court expressly reserved the standard for searches involving law enforcement
detail: In a footnote (Footnote 7), the Court's standard is framed for a search by 'a teacher or other school official,' and the Court expressly declined to decide (reserved for another day) the appropriate standard when school officials act in conjunction with or at the behest of law-enforcement officers. A different, higher standard can therefore apply once police are involved. BLOCKER constraint 3: this case is about PUBLIC-SCHOOL officials, not police.

claim: Identity of the assistant vice principal
detail: The assistant vice principal who conducted the search is named in the record as Theodore Choplick. Used only as background; narration keeps him to his role (an assistant vice principal), not a personal focus.
sources: Cornell LII, 469 U.S. 325 (opinion, Part I) — name appears in record; role is the load-bearing fact

claim: The high school was in New Jersey (Piscataway)
detail: The events occurred at a public high school in New Jersey (Piscataway High School, Middlesex County). Narration keeps to 'a public high school in New Jersey'; the specific school name is background and not load-bearing.
